problem.failure_mode: delivered dialysis dose falls below prescription when blood flow rate and dialysate flow rate cannot be sustained
problem.failure: Documented nephrology problem: maintenance hemodialysis patients receive a prescribed dialysis dose (commonly indexed as single-pool Kt/V, with guideline targets reported around 1.2-1.4 per session in the literature) that depends directly on the sustained blood flow rate through the extracorporeal circuit and the dialysate flow rate across the dialyser. When the delivered blood flow rate falls below the prescribed value (prescriptions commonly in the 300-500 mL/min range in the literature, with some reports of inadequate dose at lower effective flows), the delivered dose falls short and session time must be extended. Documented contributing factors include vascular access recirculation, arterial and venous pressure limits of the circuit, dialyser mass-transfer area and fiber bundle geometry, dialysate flow proportioning limits, and needle gauge resistance. This description is qualitative problem-domain context from the nephrology and biomedical-engineering literature; no specific incidence rates are asserted here (the engine's own retrieval must find and custody the evidence).
problem.constraint: Any intervention must deliver the prescribed dose within the arterial and venous pressure limits the extracorporeal circuit tolerates, without increasing access recirculation, without extending session time beyond the facility schedule, and without requiring replacement of the installed machine fleet.

evidence.title: Hemodialysis-related allergic reactions: a retrospective cohort study of clinical presentations, etiologies, and management.
evidence.abstract: Objective This study aimed to investigate the etiology, clinical manifestations, management strategies, and clinical outcome of hemodialysis-related allergic reactions. Methods A retrospective cohort study was conducted to analyze clinical data from patients who experienced hemodialysis-related allergic reactions at the Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University between January 2020 and December 2025. Patients undergoing maintenance hemodialysis-with no prior history of these allergic reactions-served as the control group. Their clinical characteristics and reaction profiles were systematically analyzed. Results A total of 40 cases of hemodialysis-related allergic reactions were identified as the study group. Isolated pruritus and skin rash were observed in 25 patients (62.5%); hemodialysis-related leukopenia and thrombocytopenia, in 4 cases (10.0%); and severe anaphylactic reactions, in five cases (12.5%); Five cases exhibited atypical hemodialysis-related allergic reactions (12.5%), including hypotension within 10 min of hemodialysis initiation, malaise, nausea, and vomiting. The predominant etiological factors identified were hypersensitivity to the hemodialyzer membrane (n = 11, 27.5%), AVF needles kits and hemodialysis extracorporeal circuit tubing (Ethylene Oxide Residue) (n = 27, 67.5%), and Nafamostat Mesylate (n = 2, 5%). Thorough saline pre-rinsing of the extracorporeal circuit remained the primary preventive strategy against EO-induced hypersensitivity. Switching to irradiated-sterilized acetate-membrane or wet-membrane dialyzers effectively prevented dialyzer hypersensitivity reaction. Glucocorticoid administration was effective in mitigating severe anaphylactic reactions. Patients in the study group exhibited significantly higher plasma eosinophil counts and C-reactive protein concentrations, and significantly lower hemoglobin levels, and serum albumin concentrations compared with the control group. evidence.title: Estimation of Intradialytic Blood Volume Reduction Using Hemoglobin Changes: A Prospective Validation Study of a Pragmatic Clinical Tool.
evidence.abstract: Background/Objectives: Accurate assessment of intradialytic blood volume (BV) changes is important for optimizing fluid management in hemodialysis, but continuous BV monitoring is not universally available. Hemoglobin changes reflect hemoconcentration and may provide a simple surrogate for estimating BV reduction. We prospectively evaluated a hemoglobin-based method for estimating intradialytic BV reduction compared with machine-based BV monitoring. Methods: In this prospective single-center observational study, 187 hemodialysis sessions with complete paired measurements were analyzed. Formula-based BV reduction was calculated from pre- and post-dialysis hemoglobin values and compared with machine-measured BV reduction. Agreement was assessed using Pearson correlation, predefined absolute-difference thresholds, and Bland-Altman analysis. Exploratory receiver operating characteristic analyses evaluated the ability of formula-based estimates to identify sessions with larger machine-measured BV reductions. Results: Formula-based and machine-measured BV reduction demonstrated a moderate-to-strong correlation (r = 0.645). The predefined pragmatic agreement criterion of ≥70% of measurements within ±5% was met, with 77.5% of measurements within this range. Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated a small mean bias of -1.5%, with 95% limits of agreement from -12.4% to 9.3%. Exploratory classification performance was favorable across machine-defined BV reduction thresholds, with area under curve (AUC) values ranging from 0.84 to 0.87. At the ≥8% threshold, sensitivity was 72%, specificity 85%, positive predictive value 83%, and negative predictive value 74%. Linear regression showed that 42% of variability in machine-measured BV reduction was explained by the formula-based estimate. Conclusions: A hemoglobin-based approach provides a simple approximation of intradialytic BV reduction. evidence.title: Interpreting D-Dimer and Fibrin(ogen) Degradation Products in Hemodialysis Vascular Access Surveillance.
evidence.abstract: Background Vascular access dysfunction remains a major source of morbidity and repeat procedures in maintenance hemodialysis (HD), with thrombosis as a key proximate event. D-dimer and fibrin(ogen) degradation products (FDPs) are widely available readouts of downstream fibrin(ogen) turnover, but they are not routinely used for access surveillance and are often difficult to interpret in HD. Summary This narrative review summarizes HD-specific biology relevant to fibrin turnover and synthesizes clinical evidence linking D-dimer and FDP to access outcomes across arteriovenous fistulas, grafts, and catheters. HD promotes a prothrombotic, hypofibrinolytic profile through uremia-related endothelial disturbance, chronic inflammation, and extracorporeal circuit effects. The clinical literature is mostly small and heterogeneous in assay platforms, sampling, and outcome definitions. Across cohorts, repeated pre-dialysis measurements may provide more interpretable within-patient context than single measurements, although longitudinal HD access-specific evidence remains limited. Interpretation remains constrained by assay and unit variability and by non-access-related influences such as inflammation and intercurrent illness. Accordingly, D-dimer and FDP are best used as contextual adjuncts within an imaging- and hemodynamics-based framework, interpreted alongside access flow measures, duplex ultrasound, and clinical assessment. Key messages In HD access, repeated pre-dialysis measurements may provide more interpretable within-patient context than one-off D-dimer/FDP values, although direct longitudinal evidence remains limited. Assay and unit heterogeneity, plus systemic confounding, limit portability and access-specific interpretation. Biomarkers are best read as supportive context alongside hemodynamic measures and clinical assessment, not as stand-alone surveillance tools. evidence.title: Renal replacement therapy in patients under extracorporeal membrane oxygenation: a narrative review.
evidence.abstract: Background The use of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) has expanded for severe respiratory and circulatory failure. Acute kidney injury (AKI) is one of the most frequent complications. Up to 85% of ECMO patients develop AKI and approximately half of them require renal replacement therapy (RRT) making a comprehensive understanding of both therapies and their interaction essential for patient management. However, evidence to guide ECMO-specific RRT strategies remains limited. Main body ECMO-related AKI arises from a complex interplay between patient and circuit factors that promote inflammation, endothelial injury, and tubular damage. Timing of RRT initiation in ECMO patients often relies on criteria used in the general critically ill population. Fluid overload is consistently associated with worse outcomes, and observational data suggest that earlier RRT, primarily to control fluid balance, may improve survival although randomized trials in ECMO patients are lacking. All RRT modalities can theoretically be used, but continuous techniques are preferred. RRT can be delivered via a parallel circuit using a dedicated venous catheter or integrated into the ECMO circuit. Integrated configurations reduce the need for additional vascular access and may prolong filter lifespan but require careful pressure management and team expertise to avoid alarms, hemolysis, and air embolism. Anticoagulation strategies must balance bleeding and thrombosis risk across both circuits; unfractionated heparin remains standard, while regional citrate anticoagulation can safely extend filter lifespan in selected patients although data is lacking in patients under veno-arterial ECMO. RRT during ECMO is associated with higher short-term mortality and an increased burden of chronic kidney disease among survivors. evidence.title: Synergistic action of heparin and fluid-stopping device in reducing air embolism and hemodialysis clotting: Early results from a randomized trial.
evidence.abstract: Background Entry of air into the extracorporeal circuit and inappropriate anticoagulation are significant factors associated with clotting. Even with systemic heparination, microbubbles can be implicated as sites for thrombosis and accelerate heparin metabolism. Fluid Stop devices, which prevent fluid from flowing during line drainage, have been shown potentially to decrease air embolism and improve hemostasis within circuits, but there is no concrete evidence available regarding simultaneous heparin use. Objectives The objective of this trial was to determine whether the use of systemic heparin and a portable fluid stop device can decrease air embolism and clotting within hemodialysis circuits compared with traditional infusion sets. Anticoagulation stability, risk of bleeding, and patient satisfaction were also measured. Methods In this prospectively conducted single-center randomized controlled trial, 80 hemodialysis patients receiving maintenance hemodialysis were randomly assigned either to a control group with standard infusion sets or an observation group with fluid-stopping sets and all receiving standard heparin doses. A total of 800 hemodialysis sessions were conducted prospectively with observation for air bubble entrance, line draining, and clotting. Secondary endpoints included ACT variability, satisfaction rates, and instances of bleeding complications. Results A significantly lower number of line emptying procedures (3 vs. 24; 5.0% vs. 27.5%), air bubble entries (4 vs. 28; 7.5% vs. 32.5%), and clotting incidents (2 vs. 12; 2.5% vs. 22.5%) were seen in the observation group compared with controls (P Conclusion Findings from these preliminary studies indicate that fluid-stopping devices may potentially improve heparin efficacy by preventing air embolism and clotting with no loss of safety. Based on these preliminary findings, larger multicenter trials are needed.

CROSS_DOMAIN_MIN_NONGENERIC_OVERLAP.justification: R377 patent-text ground truth (TOSCANINI/R377_PATENT_TEXT_FETCH.json + R377_PATENT_TEXT_GROUND_TRUTH.json): 12/30 family representatives (40%) were substantively irrelevant cross-domain term collisions (CWDM optical link for a battery-thermal candidate; dental-condition monitoring for rolling stock; bone fracture forceps for rail steel...). A hit sharing NO entity term with the candidate now needs >= 3 NON-generic mechanism terms to be mechanism art: the measured true cross-domain analog (line-pipe steel with hydrogen fracture toughness for a rail-steel candidate) shares 3 non-generic terms and survives; every measured false positive shares <= 2 and is demoted. This RAISES the cross-domain bar (was the same >= 2 as same-domain) — stricter, not weaker (Art. VII).

A combination qualifies only if it produces a demonstrably new technical effect that survives prior art and non-obviousness attack. A world-class invention needs a genuinely new technical information source, transformation, or control capability. Do not build an AI layer on top of an already-claimed sensing/control architecture.' NOTE: This theorem does NOT create a universal 'new sensor required' rule. A novel combination of existing measurements CAN qualify if it produces a new, technically non-obvious effect. The theorem rejects TRIVIAL recombination, not all combinations.

warnings.lesson: A signal can be GENUINELY ORTHOGONAL to a specific measurement architecture (Hakim measures pressure, not HRV) and still be a DOWNSTREAM CONSEQUENCE of the same physiological variable (ICP → sympathetic → HRV). Orthogonality to one architecture does not imply independence from the underlying physiology. Before claiming a signal is 'new information,' test whether it is causally downstream of an already-measured variable. If A → B and A is measured, then B is a proxy for A, not new information — even if B is measured by a different sensor.

Patent searches must generate terminology from patent claims + descriptions + CPC classes + inventor vocabulary + adjacent technologies, not just internally coined phrases. A query-fragile search produces false negatives.' The machine must be better at discovering what competitors actually claimed than it is at inventing elegant names for what we hope is new.

warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-016 (sharpened per CEO Round 58): A proposed latent quantity survives only when (1) identifiability is demonstrated under an EXPLICIT observation/dynamics model with full rank/observability analysis (not naive unknown-count), AND (2) identifiability REMAINS under plausible model uncertainty (each ideal assumption relaxed toward realistic physics and re-tested). A single favorable rank calculation under a convenient model is INSUFFICIENT. A single unfavorable perturbation model is ALSO INSUFFICIENT to claim universal non-identifiability — it only kills the specific estimator tested under that specific perturbation model. The correct procedure: (a) define state, observables, inputs, noise, known/unknown params; (b) build measurement equations; (c) test rank of Jacobian wrt unknown params; (d) perform adversarial model-uncertainty test: relax each assumption toward realistic physics and re-test identifiability under the combined relaxed model; (e) only if BOTH the ideal-model rank AND the adversarial-model rank hold (or constructively fail) can a universal claim (measurable OR non-measurable) be recorded.

warnings.territory: Cross-cutting (extracted from Stroke Round 58; applies to all latent-variable inventions)
warnings.mechanism: Structural identifiability under a convenient model is not enough — adversarial model-uncertainty and practical-operation survival are mandatory
warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-017: A discovery engine earns trust when it attacks its own successful proof harder than its unsuccessful ideas. Structural identifiability under a convenient model is not enough. A candidate must survive adversarial model uncertainty AND practical operation (safety, timing, decision value, first-pass vs post-hoc). The burden is bidirectional: (a) the proposer must demonstrate identifiability survives realistic model relaxation; (b) the killer must demonstrate non-identifiability holds under EVERY plausible estimator and measurement protocol, not just the one they chose to attack. When in doubt, the implementation is killed; the scientific question stays open until either (a) a survivor is found or (b) an explicit non-identifiability counterexample is constructed (two physically distinct latent states producing indistinguishable observations under ALL measurement protocols).

warnings.territory: Cross-cutting (extracted from Round 62 capability collision failure; applies to ALL novelty claims)
warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.mechanism: Minimum Sufficient Validation Evidence Derivation (MSVED) — 4-link chain: ML change → clinical pathway → risk envelope → minimum sufficient evidence → sufficiency proof
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

Methods A retrospective cohort study was conducted to analyze clinical data from patients who experienced hemodialysis-related allergic reactions at the Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University between January 2020 and December 2025. Patients undergoing maintenance hemodialysis-with no prior history of these allergic reactions-served as the control group. Their clinical characteristics and reaction profiles were systematically analyzed. Results A total of 40 cases of hemodialysis-related allergic reactions were identified as the study group. Isolated pruritus and skin rash were observed in 25 patients (62.5%); hemodialysis-related leukopenia and thrombocytopenia, in 4 cases (10.0%); and severe anaphylactic reactions, in five cases (12.5%); Five cases exhibited atypical hemodialysis-related allergic reactions (12.5%), including hypotension within 10 min of hemodialysis initiation, malaise, nausea, and vomiting. The predominant etiological factors identified were hypersensitivity to the hemodialyzer membrane (n = 11, 27.5%), AVF needles kits and hemodialysis extracorporeal circuit tubing (Ethylene Oxide Residue) (n = 27, 67.5%), and Nafamostat Mesylate (n = 2, 5%). Thorough saline pre-rinsing of the extracorporeal circuit remained the primary preventive strategy against EO-induced hypersensitivity. Switching to irradiated-sterilized acetate-membrane or wet-membrane dialyzers effectively prevented dialyzer hypersensitivity reaction. Glucocorticoid administration was effective in mitigating severe anaphylactic reactions. Patients in the study group exhibited significantly higher plasma eosinophil counts and C-reactive protein concentrations, and significantly lower hemoglobin levels, and serum albumin concentrations compared with the control group. custody_records.raw_content: Background/Objectives: Accurate assessment of intradialytic blood volume (BV) changes is important for optimizing fluid management in hemodialysis, but continuous BV monitoring is not universally available. Hemoglobin changes reflect hemoconcentration and may provide a simple surrogate for estimating BV reduction. We prospectively evaluated a hemoglobin-based method for estimating intradialytic BV reduction compared with machine-based BV monitoring. Methods: In this prospective single-center observational study, 187 hemodialysis sessions with complete paired measurements were analyzed. Formula-based BV reduction was calculated from pre- and post-dialysis hemoglobin values and compared with machine-measured BV reduction. Agreement was assessed using Pearson correlation, predefined absolute-difference thresholds, and Bland-Altman analysis. Exploratory receiver operating characteristic analyses evaluated the ability of formula-based estimates to identify sessions with larger machine-measured BV reductions. Results: Formula-based and machine-measured BV reduction demonstrated a moderate-to-strong correlation (r = 0.645). The predefined pragmatic agreement criterion of ≥70% of measurements within ±5% was met, with 77.5% of measurements within this range. Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated a small mean bias of -1.5%, with 95% limits of agreement from -12.4% to 9.3%. Exploratory classification performance was favorable across machine-defined BV reduction thresholds, with area under curve (AUC) values ranging from 0.84 to 0.87. At the ≥8% threshold, sensitivity was 72%, specificity 85%, positive predictive value 83%, and negative predictive value 74%. Linear regression showed that 42% of variability in machine-measured BV reduction was explained by the formula-based estimate. Conclusions: A hemoglobin-based approach provides a simple approximation of intradialytic BV reduction. custody_records.raw_content: Background Vascular access dysfunction remains a major source of morbidity and repeat procedures in maintenance hemodialysis (HD), with thrombosis as a key proximate event. D-dimer and fibrin(ogen) degradation products (FDPs) are widely available readouts of downstream fibrin(ogen) turnover, but they are not routinely used for access surveillance and are often difficult to interpret in HD. Summary This narrative review summarizes HD-specific biology relevant to fibrin turnover and synthesizes clinical evidence linking D-dimer and FDP to access outcomes across arteriovenous fistulas, grafts, and catheters. HD promotes a prothrombotic, hypofibrinolytic profile through uremia-related endothelial disturbance, chronic inflammation, and extracorporeal circuit effects. The clinical literature is mostly small and heterogeneous in assay platforms, sampling, and outcome definitions. Across cohorts, repeated pre-dialysis measurements may provide more interpretable within-patient context than single measurements, although longitudinal HD access-specific evidence remains limited. Interpretation remains constrained by assay and unit variability and by non-access-related influences such as inflammation and intercurrent illness. Accordingly, D-dimer and FDP are best used as contextual adjuncts within an imaging- and hemodynamics-based framework, interpreted alongside access flow measures, duplex ultrasound, and clinical assessment. Key messages In HD access, repeated pre-dialysis measurements may provide more interpretable within-patient context than one-off D-dimer/FDP values, although direct longitudinal evidence remains limited. Assay and unit heterogeneity, plus systemic confounding, limit portability and access-specific interpretation. Biomarkers are best read as supportive context alongside hemodynamic measures and clinical assessment, not as stand-alone surveillance tools. custody_records.raw_content: Background The use of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) has expanded for severe respiratory and circulatory failure. Acute kidney injury (AKI) is one of the most frequent complications. Up to 85% of ECMO patients develop AKI and approximately half of them require renal replacement therapy (RRT) making a comprehensive understanding of both therapies and their interaction essential for patient management. However, evidence to guide ECMO-specific RRT strategies remains limited. Main body ECMO-related AKI arises from a complex interplay between patient and circuit factors that promote inflammation, endothelial injury, and tubular damage. Timing of RRT initiation in ECMO patients often relies on criteria used in the general critically ill population. Fluid overload is consistently associated with worse outcomes, and observational data suggest that earlier RRT, primarily to control fluid balance, may improve survival although randomized trials in ECMO patients are lacking. All RRT modalities can theoretically be used, but continuous techniques are preferred. RRT can be delivered via a parallel circuit using a dedicated venous catheter or integrated into the ECMO circuit. Integrated configurations reduce the need for additional vascular access and may prolong filter lifespan but require careful pressure management and team expertise to avoid alarms, hemolysis, and air embolism. Anticoagulation strategies must balance bleeding and thrombosis risk across both circuits; unfractionated heparin remains standard, while regional citrate anticoagulation can safely extend filter lifespan in selected patients although data is lacking in patients under veno-arterial ECMO. RRT during ECMO is associated with higher short-term mortality and an increased burden of chronic kidney disease among survivors. custody_records.raw_content: Background Entry of air into the extracorporeal circuit and inappropriate anticoagulation are significant factors associated with clotting. Even with systemic heparination, microbubbles can be implicated as sites for thrombosis and accelerate heparin metabolism. Fluid Stop devices, which prevent fluid from flowing during line drainage, have been shown potentially to decrease air embolism and improve hemostasis within circuits, but there is no concrete evidence available regarding simultaneous heparin use. Objectives The objective of this trial was to determine whether the use of systemic heparin and a portable fluid stop device can decrease air embolism and clotting within hemodialysis circuits compared with traditional infusion sets. Anticoagulation stability, risk of bleeding, and patient satisfaction were also measured. Methods In this prospectively conducted single-center randomized controlled trial, 80 hemodialysis patients receiving maintenance hemodialysis were randomly assigned either to a control group with standard infusion sets or an observation group with fluid-stopping sets and all receiving standard heparin doses. A total of 800 hemodialysis sessions were conducted prospectively with observation for air bubble entrance, line draining, and clotting. Secondary endpoints included ACT variability, satisfaction rates, and instances of bleeding complications. Results A significantly lower number of line emptying procedures (3 vs. 24; 5.0% vs. 27.5%), air bubble entries (4 vs. 28; 7.5% vs. 32.5%), and clotting incidents (2 vs. 12; 2.5% vs. 22.5%) were seen in the observation group compared with controls (P Conclusion Findings from these preliminary studies indicate that fluid-stopping devices may potentially improve heparin efficacy by preventing air embolism and clotting with no loss of safety. Based on these preliminary findings, larger multicenter trials are needed.
